extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and graduate students writing literature reviews (academic researchers/new authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for defining and limiting the topic and scope of an academic literature review, including choices about coverage, timeframe, focus, languages, and level of detail. Helps students decide what to include and how narrowly to frame their review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to Have a Precise Topic
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that one defines a research topic very carefully. For example, the topic should not be too far-reaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly broad topics (example given: "Life and Times of Sigmund Freud" is too broad). Prefer focused, specific topics (example: "An Analysis of the Relationship of Freud and Jung in the International Psychoanalytic Association, 1910-1914").

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of Study (explicitly specify limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: In specifying precisely one's research topic, one is also specifying appropriate limitations on the research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit by time, personnel, gender, age, location, nationality, etc., to produce a more focused and meaningful topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define Exactly What Will Be Covered
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the precise scope of the literature review: what exactly will you cover in your review?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit boundaries for the subject matter so readers and you know what is inside versus outside the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide How Comprehensive the Review Will Be
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether your review will be comprehensive or selective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify whether you'll review ALL relevant material or limit the scope (for example, only recent material such as the last five years). Consider the expectations of your discipline and assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set Length / Number of Citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how long the review should be and about how many citations you will use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan approximate length and citation count ahead of time to guide searching and analysis; match scope to assignment or publication norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide Level of Detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how detailed the review will be: a broad overview or an in-depth analysis of selected works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose between summarizing many works at a surface level versus detailed critical engagement with fewer sources, depending on purpose and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the Focus of the Review (methodological/theoretical/empirical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether you will focus on methodological approaches, theoretical issues, qualitative research, quantitative research, or another axis of focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting a focus helps narrow searches and organize the review (e.g., emphasizing methods vs. theories vs. findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide Whether to Broaden to Related Disciplines
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide if you will broaden your search to include literature from related disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including related fields can provide interdisciplinary perspectives but may expand scope substantially—weigh relevance and manageability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide Language Inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether you will confine reviewed material to English only or include research in other languages too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including other languages may be important for comprehensiveness or particular topics, but consider language competence and translation resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / Currency of Sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how important timeliness (recency) is to your subject area when evaluating studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sciences generally require more recent material; arts/humanities may value older, foundational works (example: research published in 1920 about Plato might be more relevant than recent studies). Tailor currency expectations to disciplinary norms and research questions.
